highlight.title: AI's Real Threat to Jobs Is Lower Paychecks, Not Job Loss
highlight.summary: New research highlighted by Business Insider argues that AI's primary labor market impact is wage compression rather than outright displacement, suggesting workers keep their jobs but see reduced pay as AI substitutes for portions of their tasks. The finding aligns with theoretical work showing firms can retain workers while eroding the productivity rents that supported higher wages. This reframes the policy debate away from unemployment toward income inequality. (Business Insider / HN, 2026-08-01)

highlight.title: NBER: Automation Can Harm Workers Without Replacing Them — 'Replaceable but Employed'
highlight.summary: Joshua Gans (NBER w35559) models how a credible machine alternative undermines the meaning-derived component of worker utility even when the firm retains the employee, creating welfare losses invisible to standard employment statistics. The mechanism operates through the destruction of workers' sense of indispensability, not through headcount reductions. This provides a formal microfoundation for the wage-compression narrative gaining traction in empirical work.

highlight.title: Federal Reserve Publishes Real-Time Dashboard for Tracking AI Buildout and Economic Impact
highlight.summary: A new FEDS Note from Soto, Thieu, and Allen (Federal Reserve Board, 2026-07-17) organizes publicly available indicators into three categories to help researchers and policymakers monitor generative AI's macroeconomic footprint on a timely basis. The note explicitly connects capital expenditure on AI infrastructure to labor market outcomes, providing a synthesis framework for disparate data streams. Its release partially addresses the overdue Fed AI-adoption monitoring series flagged in the recurring-series tracker.

highlight.title: Cognitive Commons Framework: AI Threatens Collective Regeneration of Professional Expertise
highlight.summary: Nolan Lovett (arXiv 2607.29380) introduces the 'Cognitive Commons' concept, arguing that AI-assisted professional work may deplete the shared pool of tacit knowledge that occupations rely on to reproduce expertise across generations of workers. Unlike displacement, this mechanism operates through deskilling of the pipeline rather than direct job loss, with particularly acute risks for knowledge-intensive white-collar professions. The paper calls for HRD scholarship to treat expertise regeneration as a collective-action problem.

highlight.title: Generative AI Floods and Dilutes the Book Market, Threatening Creative-Sector Earnings
highlight.summary: An arXiv preprint (discussed on Hacker News with 104 comments, 2026-08-02) documents how generative AI is flooding book marketplaces with synthetic titles, compressing discoverability and per-unit earnings for human authors. The dilution dynamic differs from direct automation displacement: human creators remain active but face structurally lower returns as AI-generated supply expands. The findings carry direct implications for freelancer and creative-industry compensation trajectories.
